verdict.rationale: iTerm2's GitHub README documents Session Restoration. Sessions run in long-lived server processes, so after an iTerm2 crash or upgrade the shells, and with them their working directories, keep running, and iTerm2 reconnects to them 'exactly where you left off' on restart. tmux integration also reopens windows 'in the same state they were in before.' missing for 10: evidence that state survives a full machine reboot, first-party docs explicitly covering window/tab layout and working-directory restoration, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a developer, I can restore my windows, tabs, and working directories after a restart or crash

citations.quote: Session Restoration - Sessions run in long-lived server processes. If iTerm2 crashes or upgrades, your shells keep running. When iTerm2 restarts, it reconnects to your sessions exactly where you left off.
You can return to the host you were ssh'ed into and run "tmux -CC attach" and the iTerm2 windows will reopen in the same state they were in before.
